question: A utility is redrawing pressure zone boundaries across a growing city. Which input most directly decides where a boundary between two zones is placed?
correctAnswer: The ground elevation range across the service area
explanation: Zone boundaries follow elevation because elevation differences change static pressure. Hydrant counts, main age, and billing cycles do not set the hydraulic grade a zone can serve.
options: The ground elevation range across the service area
The number of hydrants installed along each street
The age of the oldest water main in the network
The billing cycle assigned to customers in the area
optionA: The ground elevation range across the service area
optionB: The number of hydrants installed along each street
optionC: The age of the oldest water main in the network
optionD: The billing cycle assigned to customers in the area

question: A senior operator wants evidence that water quality holds up at the far ends of a large network. Which data set gives that evidence most directly?
correctAnswer: Chlorine residual and sample results from extremity sites
explanation: Extremity and dead-end sites show the oldest water in the system, so their residuals and sample results reveal whether quality survives distribution. Plant outlet results only describe water before it travels.

Pump run hours recorded at the main booster station
Customer billing totals grouped by neighbourhood area

question: An elevated tank fills at night and drains during the day through one riser pipe. Which condition makes that single pipe work in both directions?
correctAnswer: System pressure rising above and falling below tank head
explanation: When system pressure exceeds the head from the tank water level, water flows in; when demand pulls system pressure below that head, water flows out. No separate fill and drain lines are needed.
options: A check valve holding the riser at a fixed pressure
System pressure rising above and falling below tank head
The overflow pipe carrying the normal daily exchange
A second tank balancing every level change in the first

Close the zone boundary valves to hold the water longer

question: A booster station uses more energy per cubic metre than its twin station. Which operating condition most often explains that gap?
correctAnswer: The pump runs far from its best efficiency point
explanation: A pump forced to operate well away from its best efficiency point converts far less input energy into useful water movement. Run timing, motor age, and main length alone do not explain a large unit energy gap.

The discharge main is shorter than the twin station main

question: An operator runs two identical pumps in parallel to meet a modest demand that one pump could carry alone. What is the most likely energy consequence?
correctAnswer: Each pump works off its efficient point and unit energy rises
explanation: Splitting a modest flow between two pumps pushes each one left of its best efficiency point, so more energy is spent per cubic metre delivered. One pump near its duty point is usually the efficient choice.

Station energy stays identical regardless of the pump count
